slides.0.title: Course Introduction
slides.0.content:
Vineyard management is the foundation of wine quality. From winter pruning to balance yield and quality, to summer green harvesting to control grape quantities, to autumn harvest to capture perfect ripeness — every decision influences the final wine style. In Bordeaux, these traditional skills are being deeply integrated with modern sustainable agriculture principles.

This course takes you deep into the annual work cycle and decision-making logic of Bordeaux vineyards, and explores the scientific principles and practical challenges of the three major systems: organic farming, biodynamic farming, and sustainable agriculture. From the pioneering biodynamic practices of Château Pontet-Canet to the growing number of classified growths receiving HVE certification, sustainable agriculture has become Bordeaux's future direction.

Course Learning Objectives

📅 Master the Annual Management Cycle

Understand the timing and techniques of key tasks: winter pruning, spring bud-break management, summer green harvesting, and autumn harvest

🌱 In-depth Understanding of Three Sustainable Systems

Learn the differences in principles, certification standards, and practical challenges among organic farming, biodynamic farming, and sustainable agriculture

🐛 Learn Integrated Pest Management

Master modern IPM (Integrated Pest Management) methods to reduce chemical use while protecting yields

✅ Analyse the Three Certification Systems

Understand the standards and significance of Organic Certification (AB), Biodynamic Certification (Demeter), and High Environmental Value Certification (HVE)

⚖️ Evaluate the Multi-dimensional Impact of Sustainable Agriculture

Analyse the combined effects on wine quality, production costs, market value, and environmental impact

On completing this course, you will have a comprehensive understanding of the science and art of modern vineyard management, and how sustainable agriculture is shaping Bordeaux's future.

Estimated study time: 55 minutes

Difficulty level: Advanced Professional

slides.4.question: Why are both winter pruning (January) and green harvesting (July) considered key moments in 'yield management'?
slides.4.options.0: Both directly remove fruit, reducing yields
slides.4.options.1: Winter pruning sets the potential yield ceiling; green harvesting adjusts actual yield to optimise quality
slides.4.options.2: Both are aimed at disease prevention, indirectly affecting yields
slides.4.options.3: Winter pruning increases yield while green harvesting reduces it, balancing the two
slides.4.explanation: Winter pruning controls the number of fruiting canes and buds, setting the potential yield ceiling for the year from the outset. For example, retaining 8 fruiting canes vs. 12 can result in a yield difference of up to 50%. However, actual fruit set may exceed expectations (under ideal flowering conditions), or the estate may be pursuing higher quality. Green harvesting in July (before véraison), by thinning excess or poor-quality bunches, adjusts the actual yield to the target level (top estates typically target 35–40 hl/ha). This ensures that the remaining grapes can ripen fully and reach optimal concentration. Together, the two reflect a philosophy of meticulous management: 'source-level control + later-stage optimisation'.

slides.7.description: The principles and practice of organic farming: a return to nature
slides.8.title: Organic Farming ① Core Principles
slides.8.content:
📖 Core Principles Explained

Organic farming is built on five core principles:

  • No synthetic chemical pesticides or fertilisers: Return to natural methods, using compost, green manure, and other organic matter
  • No Genetically Modified Organisms (GMO): Protect biodiversity and natural evolution
  • Promote biodiversity: Create healthy ecosystems where natural predators control pests and diseases
  • Protect soil, water, and animal welfare: Maintain environmental health with a long-term perspective
  • Build a closed-loop system: Self-sufficient within the vineyard, reducing dependence on external inputs

💡 Key philosophy: work with nature, not against it
slides.9.title: Organic Farming ② Permitted vs. Prohibited Practices
slides.9.content:
📖 Permitted and Prohibited Practices Explained

✅ Permitted

Fertilisers: Compost, green manure, bone meal, fish meal, and other natural organic matter

Disease Control: Copper (≤4 kg/ha/year), sulphur, plant extracts, biological agents

Weed Management: Mechanical weeding, manual weeding, cover crops

❌ Strictly Prohibited

All synthetic chemical pesticides (insecticides, fungicides, herbicides)

Synthetic chemical fertilisers (NPK fertilisers)

Herbicides (e.g. Glyphosate)

Genetically modified organisms (GMO seeds, rootstocks)

⚠️ Key challenge: copper use restrictions may be insufficient to control downy mildew in wet years
slides.10.title: Organic Farming ③ Certification Process and Requirements
slides.10.content:
📖 Certification Process in Detail

🏆 Main Certification Logos

EU Organic: EU organic certification — green leaf logo

AB (Agriculture Biologique): France's official organic certification

⏱️ Conversion Period (3 years)

Year 0: Decision to convert; stop using synthetic chemicals

Years 1–3: Operating under organic methods, but cannot label as organic (costs incurred, no market premium yet)

Year 3+: Certification obtained; may label wines as organic

📋 Ongoing Requirements
  • Annual unannounced inspections by a third-party body
  • Detailed records of all farm operations and inputs
  • Testing for residues of prohibited substances (grapes and soil)
  • Certification fees + annual inspection fees (several thousand euros)

💡 The conversion period is the greatest economic challenge: costs increase but cannot label as organic
slides.11.title: Organic Farming ④ Challenge Analysis
slides.11.content:
📖 Challenge Analysis Across Three Dimensions

🔧 Technical Challenges
  • Disease control difficulty: Copper use limits (≤4 kg/ha/year) insufficient in wet years (e.g. the 2018 downy mildew outbreak)
  • Labour-intensive weed control: Mechanical or manual weeding is costly and time-consuming
  • Possible yield decline: 10–20% in the initial conversion period; requires more intensive monitoring
💰 Economic Challenges
  • Labour costs increase 30–50%: Greatly increased needs for weeding, monitoring, and manual operations
  • Yield decline pushes up unit costs: Production cost per bottle rises significantly
  • Conversion period dilemma: Costs incurred for 3 years but cannot label as organic or command a market premium
  • Equipment investment: Mechanical weeders, precision spraying equipment (tens of thousands of euros)
🌦️ Climate Challenges

Extremely difficult in wet years: High pressure from downy mildew and powdery mildew; copper allowance quickly exhausted (many organic estates suffered severe losses in 2018)

Actually advantageous in dry years: Low disease pressure; organic advantages come into play (organic estates excelled in 2020)

⚠️ Conclusion: organic farming is more challenging in Bordeaux's oceanic climate (rainy) than in a Mediterranean climate
slides.12.title: Organic Farming ⑤ Comprehensive Benefits
slides.12.content:
📖 Benefit Analysis Across Three Dimensions

🌍 Environmental Benefits
  • Soil health: Protects microbial diversity; long-term improvement of soil fertility and structure
  • Reduced pollution: Protects water sources from chemical contamination
  • Biodiversity: Insects, birds, and plant species increase markedly; ecological balance restored
  • Sustainability: Preserving healthy land resources for future generations
🍷 Wine Quality Benefits

Flavour purity: Theoretically purer terroir expression (debated)

Antioxidant content: Some research shows higher levels in organic grapes

Consumer perception: 'Healthy', 'natural' image aligned with modern values

⚠️ Note: organic ≠ automatically high quality; excellent viticulture and winemaking skills are still required

💎 Market Benefits
  • Price premium of 15–30%: Premium markets willing to pay more for organic certification
  • Target audience: Attracts environmentally conscious, health-seeking consumers
  • Brand differentiation: Establishes a distinctive position in a competitive market
  • Storytelling: The organic conversion journey becomes a compelling brand narrative

💡 Finding balance: environmental benefits are long-term; economic benefits take 3–5 years to materialise
slides.13.title: Organic Farming ⑥ Adoption Trends in Bordeaux
slides.13.content:
📖 Development History of Organic Farming in Bordeaux

📊 Adoption Rate Timeline
  • 2000: <1% — organic farming almost non-existent
  • 2010: 3% — pioneering estates begin exploration
  • 2020: 15% — period of rapid growth
  • 2023: 18% (certified or in conversion) — an important trend
  • 2030 target: France's national goal is 18% organic; Bordeaux aims to exceed this
🏆 Pioneer Estates

Château Pontet-Canet (2010): A Pauillac classified estate; fully converted to organic and received Biodyvin certification; significant quality improvement

Château Palmer (2008): A Margaux Third Growth; organic + biodynamic practice

Château Climens (2010): A Barsac First Growth; received Demeter certification

The success of these top estates proves that organic farming and high quality can go hand in hand

🔍 Adoption Pattern Observations

Scale effect: Larger estates more easily absorb conversion costs (capital, labour, risk buffers)

Drivers: Consumer environmental awareness, brand differentiation, beliefs of the new generation of winemakers, government subsidy policies

Growth trend: Continued rapid growth; organic farming is evolving from a 'niche experiment' to a 'regional mainstream'

🌟 Outlook: it is anticipated that by 2030 the organic vineyard area in Bordeaux will reach 25–30%

slides.15.title: Knowledge Check: Sustainable Agriculture
slides.15.question: Why did many organic estates struggle in 2018 (a wet vintage), while organic estates excelled in 2020 (a dry vintage)?
slides.15.options.0: Organic pesticides were ineffective in 2018, but more effective in 2020
slides.15.options.1: Wet conditions in 2018 caused downy mildew outbreaks but copper use limits were insufficient for control; dry conditions in 2020 meant extremely low disease pressure
slides.15.options.2: Organic vines were too young in 2018 but had matured by 2020
slides.15.options.3: The market did not recognise organic in 2018, but acceptance increased by 2020
slides.15.explanation: This perfectly illustrates the climate dependency of organic farming. Spring and summer 2018 were unusually wet and warm — ideal conditions for downy mildew. Organic estates could only use copper-based products (Bordeaux mixture) for control, but EU regulations limit copper to ≤4 kg/ha/year. In an extremely wet vintage, this quantity is insufficient to control the disease (which may require 10–15 applications, but the copper allowance is quickly exhausted), resulting in widespread vineyard infection and reduced yields and quality. In contrast, the summer of 2020 was dry, with very low disease pressure and almost no need for control treatments, allowing organic estates to fully leverage their advantages (healthy soil, biodiversity, no chemical residues). This is also why many experts believe organic farming is more difficult to implement in Bordeaux's oceanic climate (rainy) than in a Mediterranean climate.
